reviews.text: Once you stop playing KAZ you don’t stop playing KAZ because the fifteen-second timer is ticking down and in this ambitiously minimalistic twist on whack-a-mole you have keep moving from square to square, maximizing your actions-per-minute (APM) by smashing the highest-value targets while dodging traps and casting spells—and OK, yes, you do get a break between rounds where you can consider which power-up will synergize best with your chosen character’s abilities (or which debuff you can live with if you’ve been carelessly stomping on trap tiles), but this is a game that revels not only in calculating your APM but its effectivity, which is to say, whether you’re always moving toward a target—and so but then anyway, the point is that when you’re moving, you’re really moving, and while it’s neat to see Balatro played a high-level at GDQ, there you’ve got a pre-set strategy and you can plan for the upcoming blinds, and in KAZ you’ve just got to keep reacting (usually poorly) to all the chaos that’s developing around you; and there is a method behind all that madness, because as you continue to complete in-game challenges, you’ll unlock abilities that basically let you hack the whack-a-mole board, from minor conveniences like forcing enemies to spawn more frequently, or closer to your position, to spells that you can cast by pressing a certain series of inputs, like down down down up in order to invert every tile, such that if every square were blank, now every square has an enemy on it—oh, and these abilities are funny, like the way in which Crypto Guy increases the value of every enemy you attack but only up until you hit your first wall, or the way in which the Three Body Problem debuff will obnoxiously display the end-round timer in the middle of the screen, slightly obscuring your vision—and I marvel a bit at how easy KAZ is to interpret even at high speeds, because it really is a classic arcade game with only three enemies (static, moving, shielded), one kind of trap, and the occasional high-valued star to collect (assuming that’s a power-up you’ve chosen), which leaves you safe to try and manage all the power-ups, like a disco ball that turns each stage into Crypt of the Necrodancer, giving extra points for each foe hit while on a lit square, or to remember on what move your chosen weapon is going to activate—and in fact, part of KAZ‘s addictive “one more run” charm (apart from the brevity) stems from all the unique skins you can unlock, such that Rhythm Doctor unsurprisingly earns bonus points from every seventh enemy (all of which look like beats on a heart monitor) while Christophe Galati’s character from Save me Mr Tako can dig an extra tile each round (while stylishly slaying various octopi in black and white)—which is all to say that while not every character or ability seems equally powerful and you’re certainly at the vicissitudes of whether you’re offered enough ways to increase your score before the cap exceeds your APM capabilities, because these are at most five minute mad-dash score rushes with so many striking aesthetics to shift through, KAZ kept surprising me more than irking me and if the game felt unfair it never felt unfun which is really what you’re looking for when you’re just trying to let off some Steam.

While I highly recommend it I think it's important to disclose this is much more arcade game experience than a typical roguelike. The gameplay is fast and frenetic with no real incentive outside of score and unlocks. It has a very "insert quarter to play instantly and get on the leaderboard" feel. Don't go expecting any type of narrative or even a true win state. As well as I think it be even more fun with an arcade joystick than a controller or keyboard (but I have yet to test that). But what it is, the gameplay is great. It's easy to pick up but hard to master. Lots of fun.

I booted this up thinking "cute little arcade game, I'll play for 20 minutes." That was several hours ago. My fingers hate me. KAZ is basically whack-a-mole on crack with a roguelike card system slapped on top. You smash WASD to kill enemies on a grid before the timer runs out, grab cards between rounds to build your score, and then do it all again because the game over screen has the audacity to look really cool and make you want one more run. It's pure unfiltered dopamine in a tiny package and I am not okay. The visuals and sound design are genuinely juicy in a way that's hard to describe. Every hit feels satisfying, the lasers and lightning effects go absolutely hard, and each character completely changes how the game looks and plays. There are apparently 20+ unlockable themes too which is wild for something this cheap. My only gripe is that later rounds start feeling more like "did you get the right cards" than actual skill expression, which can sting a little. But honestly by that point you're so hooked you'll just start another run immediately anyway. At under seven euros this is embarrassingly good value. Quick sessions, massive replayability, and the perfect game for when your brain needs something loud and fast and shiny. This is a very fun, stylish, and easy to pick up and put down game. Perfect for when you have ten or fifteen minutes to spare and a keyboard at hand. I do wish that the game did a better job at explaining keywords and the like. For example, I still have no idea what critical hits do and can't find any explanations in game. Also the balance feels a little off and punishing. I tend to have the experience of getting cut short right as I'm starting to get a build to come online. Other than those two gripes though, which could be addressed in future patches, it's a solid pick, especially for the price.

Kaz is sheer proof that simplicity can meet ambition. Four buttons, nonstop speed and explosions. That's it. Enough to make you wonder what kind of evil, yet brilliant, mind came up with this. As soon as you finish a session, you're already longing for the next one, hoping it'll go a little further than the last. That "one more run" pull is the beating heart of the game. And it beats hard. It's not enough to make you crush your keyboard and train your hand beyond reason; the sound effects also do their part to make your heart beat dangerously. But Kaz isn't only reflexes, it's also about taking decisions: which item, which spell, which malus to swallow when your curse gauge fills up. And that's where it gets you. Better is the enemy of good: reaching for the perfect run instead of the safe one is exactly how you miss power and get thrown back to round one. What carries you through is pure determination, the game quietly rewards those who refuse to stop. Bottom line: it's a gem I'll be playing with more and more intensity.
